stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, Public Law 89-236.
stimulus.text:
Paraphrase of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, also called the Hart-Celler Act. The act abolished the national quota system based on national origins that had been in place since the 1920s. It set overall limits instead: 170,000 immigrants a year from the Eastern Hemisphere and, for the first time, 120,000 a year from the Western Hemisphere. Family members of people already in the United States were exempt from the limits, and preference went to immigrants with needed skills.

In the years that followed, migration from Asia, Africa, and Latin America rose sharply.

rationales.general:
1. The act ended quotas based on national origins.
2. Ending one kind of limit does not mean ending all limits.
3. The act set new overall limits: 170,000 and 120,000 a year.
4. Immigration therefore stayed limited, only on a new basis.
5. The new basis was family ties and needed skills, not the nation of birth.
Remember: A new limit is still a limit.
